title: Low Latency and Efficient Voice Activator for Edge Devices
department: Department of Space / Indian Space Research Organisation
description:
Background As voice-controlled IoT proliferate, processing everything in the cloud is too costly, privacy-invasive, and slow. The future belongs to hybrid architectures where the edge handles the initial 'wake-up' and the cloud handles the heavy lifting.
Description Build an ultra-lightweight, highly accurate keyword spotting (KWS) model that runs locally on a low-power device. Upon detecting the keyword, the system must instantly and efficiently stream the subsequent audio to a remote Automated Speech Recognition (ASR) server with minimal data overhead and latency.
Key Metrics for Evaluation
• Efficiency: Model size (RAM/Flash footprint) and CPU usage during idle listening.
• Accuracy: High true-positive rate for the keyword with near-zero false activations.
• Latency: The time delta between the keyword ending and the cloud ASR receiving the audio stream.
Software & Framework Restrictions
• Open-Source Only: The use of proprietary, closed-source, or commercial voice-activation SDKs is strictly prohibited.
• Allowed Frameworks: Teams must build their keyword spotting (KWS) pipelines using open-source machine learning and TinyML frameworks. Recommended tools include TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers, PyTorch Mobile or similar.
• No Pre-Trained Global Keywords: Teams cannot use models pre-trained on generic smart-assistant keywords like 'Hey Google' or 'Alexa'. They need to train on a custom key word.
Expected Solution Teams are expected to deliver a robust, deployable system architecture. A successful submission must strictly satisfy the following technical boundaries:
• Hardware & Runtime Environment: The edge software application must run smoothly within an environment restricted to less than 256KB of RAM and consume under 10% CPU utilization while idling in continuous listening mode. Heavy or uncompressed pre-trained transformers are disqualified. Solutions will be formally evaluated on physical low-power microcontrollers (e.g., Raspberry Pi or ESP32).
• Model should work for the given custom key word.
summary: Innovation (4/5): draws on machine learning, iot applied to a miscellaneous problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (2/5): as a hardware build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Miscellaneous. Tech Depth (4/5): centers on model, architecture. Sustainability (4/5): has a clear long-term maintenance path. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 18/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: Low Latency and Efficient Voice Activator for Edge Devices

overview.in_plain_terms: Build the 'wake word' layer of a voice assistant, the tiny always-on model that sits on a microcontroller listening for one custom keyword, then hands off to the cloud for the actual speech recognition once it hears it.
overview.why_it_matters: Every always-listening device (smart speakers, industrial controllers, wearables) needs something cheap and private running 24/7 at the edge, because streaming raw audio to the cloud constantly is expensive, slow, and a privacy problem. This PS is that missing piece, done properly, not as a toy demo.
pain_points: Cloud-only voice pipelines mean every whispered word gets sent off-device, that's a privacy and bandwidth cost nobody wants running continuously.
Generic wake-word engines ('Hey Google', 'Alexa') are explicitly banned here, teams have to train their own keyword detector from scratch.
The hardware budget is brutal: under 256KB RAM and under 10% CPU while idling, that rules out almost every off-the-shelf model architecture.
overview.background: As voice-controlled IoT devices spread, always-on cloud processing is too costly, too slow, and too privacy-invasive. The expected pattern is a hybrid architecture: a tiny model on the device handles the wake-up, and the cloud handles the heavy transcription work only after that.
overview.whats_being_asked: An ultra-lightweight, highly accurate keyword-spotting (KWS) model that runs locally on a low-power device, and on detection, streams the following audio to a remote ASR server with minimal latency and data overhead.
expected_solution: A custom-trained KWS model built with open-source TinyML frameworks (TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers, PyTorch Mobile, or similar), no pretrained generic-assistant keywords allowed.
Runs within under 256KB RAM and under 10% CPU while idle-listening, on physical low-power hardware like an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi.
A fast, low-overhead audio streaming handoff to a remote ASR endpoint the instant the keyword is detected.
Demonstrated accuracy: high true-positive rate on the custom keyword with near-zero false activations.
Measured latency between keyword-end and the cloud ASR server receiving the stream.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough band, but the innovation isn't the ML model itself, keyword spotting is a known technique, it's fitting a genuinely accurate custom KWS model inside a 256KB RAM budget on real hardware and proving it under the judges' own test conditions. Most 'AI on a microcontroller' hackathon projects fake this with a beefier board or a bigger model; this PS explicitly won't let you.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. You're not just training a model, you're quantizing it to fit an embedded footprint, flashing it to a physical microcontroller, and building a second-stage streaming pipeline to a cloud ASR service, all three have to work together live.

competitive_landscape.note: TinyML/edge-AI PS types are less common at SIH than generic 'AI dashboard' problems, and the hard constraint (open-source only, no pretrained keywords, strict RAM ceiling) will filter out teams unwilling to do real embedded work, expect a smaller but more technically serious field.

innovation.note: Keyword spotting is a known problem class, the innovation is squeezing it into the stated hardware envelope, not inventing new ML.

invention.note: Custom dataset collection, model training, quantization, embedded deployment, and a networked handoff pipeline is a lot of distinct engineering for 36 hours.

technical_feasibility.note: 256KB RAM and sub-10% idle CPU on real hardware (not a simulator) is an unforgiving constraint, budget serious time for on-device debugging, not just model training.

impact_and_benefits.note: This isn't a flashy end-user demo, it's a building block. Judges who understand edge AI will rate it highly; judges looking for a splashy user-facing story may undervalue it, know your audience.

architecture.note: Edge inference and cloud ASR are two separate systems with a network seam between them, that handoff is exactly where demos break during Q&A.

overall_verdict.reasoning: A strong pick for a team with embedded-systems comfort and someone who can actually flash and debug a microcontroller live, not just prototype in a Colab notebook. The strict, quantifiable requirements (RAM, CPU, latency) work in your favor at demo time: you can show hard numbers instead of vague claims.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: The requirements are unusually precise (exact RAM ceiling, exact CPU ceiling, explicit ban on pretrained keywords), which means you know exactly what to optimize for and exactly how to prove it on stage.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Teams that develop only in a simulator and never actually flash the model to physical hardware before demo day risk discovering the RAM/CPU numbers don't hold up live, in front of the judges.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm hour 0: do you have the actual target hardware (ESP32 / Raspberry Pi) in hand, and has anyone on the team flashed a TFLite Micro model to it before? If not, budget real time for that learning curve, it eats hours fast.

idea_0_4: Pick your custom keyword and record 200-500 samples fast (team members' own voices, varied distance/noise), this dataset is your bottleneck, start collecting immediately.
Confirm the exact target board and get a 'hello world' TFLite Micro model flashed and running before touching your real model, this de-risks the hardest unknown early.
Decide the cloud ASR endpoint now (open-source Whisper.cpp or similar), don't leave that integration to hour 30.
prototype_4_22: Train a small KWS model (MFCC features + a compact CNN or DS-CNN architecture) on your custom dataset, quantize to int8 immediately, don't wait to optimize later.
Get it running on-device against a stopwatch: measure actual RAM/flash footprint and idle CPU usage, this is your core evaluation metric, verify it early and often.
Build the streaming handoff: on detection, open a connection and push audio to your ASR endpoint with minimal buffering delay.
integration_22_30: Wire the full loop end to end: idle listening -> keyword detected -> stream to ASR -> transcription returned, and time every stage.
Stress-test false activations with background noise, TV audio, other speech, tune your detection threshold against real false-positive data, not guesses.
Log your measured numbers (RAM, CPU%, latency) automatically so you have hard evidence ready, not just claims, for the demo.
polish_30_36: Prepare a live on-stage demo on the actual physical hardware, not a laptop simulation, this PS's whole point is that it runs on the real device.
Build a simple dashboard or LED/serial output showing RAM/CPU numbers in real time next to the demo, so judges see the constraint being met, not just hear about it.
Rehearse the failure case: what happens with unexpected background noise, have an answer ready, don't let it be a surprise.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Bring the actual hardware and run the demo on it live, with the measured RAM/CPU/latency numbers visible on screen. Teams who only show a laptop simulation will lose credibility instantly against a team who can hand a judge the board.

strengths: Precise, quantifiable success criteria mean less ambiguity about what 'done' looks like.
A working demo is inherently convincing, it's hardware you can physically hand to a judge.
weaknesses: High dependency on embedded/firmware skills that not every team has.
Custom dataset collection under time pressure risks a model that's accurate on your own voices but brittle on others.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: 2 ML/embedded-leaning to 1 backend, this PS lives or dies on the on-device work, not the cloud side.
team_fit.approach: Split ownership by hour 0: one person owns the model+quantization pipeline, one owns the physical device flashing and constraint-measurement, one owns the ASR handoff. Merge and test on real hardware from hour 12 onward, not hour 30.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Boilerplate for MFCC feature extraction, a baseline TFLite Micro training script, and the cloud ASR client code can all be scaffolded quickly with AI coding assistance.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Dataset quality, quantization tradeoffs (accuracy vs footprint), and false-positive threshold tuning need real human listening and iteration, no AI shortcut replaces actually testing the mic in a noisy room.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-generated model architecture that was never validated against the actual 256KB constraint on real hardware will fail the moment you flash it, this PS punishes untested assumptions immediately and visibly.

data_resource_availability.status: You must generate your own keyword dataset, no public dataset satisfies the 'no pretrained generic keywords' rule; a handful of open ambient-noise datasets exist for negative samples.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: If your custom dataset is too small for good accuracy by hour 20, augment aggressively (pitch shift, noise injection, time-stretch) on your existing recordings rather than trying to collect more samples under time pressure.

judge_qna.question: Why not just use an existing open-source wake-word engine like Porcupine?
judge_qna.strong_answer: The brief explicitly bans pretrained generic-assistant keywords, we trained our own from scratch specifically to meet that constraint and to show the model choices we made to hit the RAM budget.
judge_qna.follow_up: What specific architecture and quantization choices let you hit 256KB, and what did you have to cut to get there?

judge_qna.question: How does this handle a noisy environment, like a factory floor or crowded room?
judge_qna.strong_answer: We trained with augmented background noise and tuned our detection threshold against a measured false-positive rate, here are the actual numbers from our testing.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your false-positive rate in your noisiest test condition, and is that acceptable for a real deployment?

judge_qna.question: What happens if the network connection to the cloud ASR drops right after the keyword is detected?
judge_qna.strong_answer: We buffer briefly and retry, and the wake detection itself stays fully local so the device doesn't need connectivity until the handoff moment.
judge_qna.follow_up: How long can you buffer before you'd need to fall back to an on-device transcription, even a degraded one?
